mendokoro-honda.order_how: 🔴 Ticket machine, and the rule is not the obvious one. The machine stands OUTSIDE the shop, but you do NOT buy first — signs on the wall ask you to join the back of the queue with no ticket. A member of staff comes down the line and asks whether you have bought one; that is your cue to step out, buy, and return to your place. The machine takes cards, Suica and QR.
mendokoro-honda.order: Shōyu ramen — the flagship bowl. A tare blended from five soy sauces over a broth drawn from chicken, pork, dried sardine and clam, with thin noodles cut in-house from three Japanese wheat flours.
mendokoro-honda.order_jp: 醤油ラーメンを ひとつ お願いします
mendokoro-honda.order_romaji: Shōyu rāmen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
mendokoro-honda.order_why: The Chiyoda tourism board and the shop's own reputation both put this bowl first — it is the one the place is built on. The machine offers five bases (shōyu, shōyu tsukemen, shio, shio tsukemen, tantanmen); the plain shōyu button is the one to press on a first visit.
mendokoro-honda.order_backup: If you want it richer, tokusei shōyu ramen (特製醤油ラーメン) is the same bowl with seven slices of chāshū, a soft-boiled marinated egg and better nori. ⚑ The shop's other draw, shio tsukemen (塩つけ麺), is cold noodles dipped in kombu water with sea salt and a sudachi lime — a summer order, and all three of the evenings you might be here are late October or November, so it is named for completeness rather than recommended.

kamayoshi.order_how: Order at the counter — staff take it, no ticket machine. Cards, Suica and QR are all accepted. Fourteen seats and no reservations. ⚠ Two things the shop asks in writing: it has no storage, so do not arrive with the trolley — leave luggage at the hotel first; and at weekday lunch it asks you to free the table 20–30 minutes after eating. Neither applies if you go at dinner.
kamayoshi.order: Gobō-ten udon — a whole burdock root in tempura batter, fried to order, laid across the noodles.
kamayoshi.order_jp: ごぼう天うどんを ひとつ お願いします
kamayoshi.order_romaji: Gobō-ten udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kamayoshi.order_why: The shop is a deliberate hybrid: Sanuki noodles, which are thick and hard-chewed, in the softer Hakata-style dashi. It names four bowls as its mainstays — beef, burdock tempura, fishcake, and chicken-chikuwa tempura — and the burdock is the one the reports single out, because the tempura is fried after you order and arrives still crackling.
kamayoshi.order_backup: Niku udon (肉うどん), the sweet-simmered beef bowl, is the other half of the shop's reputation. Maru-ten udon (丸天うどん), with a round fried fishcake, is the plainest and the most Hakata.

tonkatsu-marugo.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no IC, no QR. Bring notes. Table service, no reservations. ⚑ The queue here is a lunch phenomenon, not an evening one — reports put about 29 people waiting for the 11:30 lunch opening against two at 16:50 for the 17:00 dinner opening, so arrive at the open and it costs ten minutes rather than forty. Adding the set (定食) for a few hundred yen turns the cutlet into a meal with rice, pickles and red-miso soup, and the rice and cabbage are then refillable free.
tonkatsu-marugo.order: Toku-rōsu katsu — the premium loin cutlet, thick-cut, with a fat edge left on.
tonkatsu-marugo.order_jp: 特ロースかつ定食を ひとつ お願いします
tonkatsu-marugo.order_romaji: Toku-rōsu katsu teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tonkatsu-marugo.order_why: Frying here is a production line with one person per job, and the two cutlets the shop is judged on are the premium loin and the premium fillet. The loin is the fattier and the more talked-about; it is what a Michelin Bib Gourmand and five Hyakumeiten selections were given for.
tonkatsu-marugo.order_backup: Toku-hire katsu (特ヒレかつ) is the same cooking on the lean fillet — no fat edge, a little more money, and the choice if you would rather not chew through pork fat at the end of a long day.

ponta-honke.order_how: Table service across three floors; the ground floor is a three-seat counter and the rest is upstairs. Cards are accepted. ⚠ Reservations are taken only for two or more, so on your own it is walk-in — go early rather than late. Closed Mondays.
ponta-honke.order: Katsuretsu — a pale, pork-fillet cutlet cooked in lard at low temperature, closer to a French côtelette than to modern tonkatsu.
ponta-honke.order_jp: カツレツを ひとつ お願いします
ponta-honke.order_why: This is where the dish comes from. The house opened in 1905 under a founder who had cooked Western food in the Imperial Household kitchen, and its katsuretsu is the ancestor that later became tonkatsu everywhere else — trimmed of all fat, fried gently, served without the heavy sauce. Ordering anything else here is ordering around the reason to come.
ponta-honke.order_backup: Beef stew (ビーフシチュー) is the other dish the kitchen is known for. In late October and November the fried oysters (カキフライ) are in season, which is the one time of year they beat both.

delhi-ueno.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money. Fifteen seats, counter and small tables, no reservations, and it runs straight through from late morning to half nine, so an awkward hour is fine here.
delhi-ueno.order: Kashmir curry — jet-black, soup-thin, poured over rice. Very hot, and hot in a clean way rather than a blunt one.
delhi-ueno.order_jp: カシミールカレーを ひとつ お願いします
delhi-ueno.order_romaji: Kashmīru karē o hitotsu onegai shimasu
delhi-ueno.order_why: The shop has been on this corner since 1956 and this is the curry it is famous for; its own menu marks it four chillies out of five. It is thin enough to drink and much hotter than it looks, which is the whole point of the dish.
delhi-ueno.order_backup: ⚠ If four-out-of-five heat is not what you want after a long day, Indo curry (インドカレー) is the mild, thicker, more conventional bowl, and Delhi curry (デリーカレー) sits between the two.

gonokami-seisakusho.order_how: 🔴 Ticket machine, and 🔴 CASH ONLY. The machine is INSIDE, and what you do depends on whether there is a line: if the pavement outside is clear, walk in and buy at the machine; if people are waiting on the street, join the end and let staff call you in — do not walk past a line to the machine. ⚑ At the hour this day arrives there is usually no line. ⚑ When you hand the ticket over you are asked one question: nami-mori or ko-mori (並盛 / 小盛), regular or small portion. Say 'nami-mori' for regular.
gonokami-seisakusho.order: Ebi tsukemen — cold noodles you dip into a hot, almost sauce-thick soup made from a large quantity of sweet shrimp.
gonokami-seisakusho.order_jp: 海老つけ麺を ひとつ お願いします
gonokami-seisakusho.order_romaji: Ebi tsukemen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
gonokami-seisakusho.order_why: The shop calls itself a prawn-tsukemen specialist and this is the base bowl the other versions are built on. The broth is thickened with the shrimp themselves rather than with stock, which is why it coats the noodles instead of running off them.
gonokami-seisakusho.order_backup: Ebi tomato tsukemen (海老トマトつけ麺) turns the same broth sharper and is the one regulars switch to; ebi miso tsukemen (海老味噌つけ麺) makes it heavier. A flavoured egg (味玉) is the topping to add if you add one.

fish-shinjuku.order_how: Table service, twenty-six seats, walk-in. ⚠ It states that it is not taking online reservations, and the only booking channel it names is a phone one — so treat this as walk-in only; evening walk-ins are seated on dated reports. Cards, Suica and QR are all accepted. It closes between three and five, so this is a lunch or an evening meal, not a mid-afternoon one.
fish-shinjuku.order: Three-curry combo — chicken, keema and a lentil dal, served together on one plate with rice and a spread of pickles and sides.
fish-shinjuku.order_jp: 3種コンボを ひとつ お願いします
fish-shinjuku.order_romaji: Sanshu konbo o hitotsu onegai shimasu
fish-shinjuku.order_why: The combo plate is this shop's format rather than a sampler for tourists — the three curries are meant to be eaten against each other and against the sides. The kitchen carries on a Roppongi curry house that ran for about thirty years before reopening here, and the spicing is built to be distinctive without being punishing.
fish-shinjuku.order_backup: The two-curry combo (2種コンボ) is the same idea, smaller. ⚑ Take the three unless you want less: the only day this shop is on is the Takao one, whose lunch is onigiri carried up the mountain, so you will not be arriving full.

rokurinsha.order_how: 🔴 Ticket machine, pay first — cash and transport IC both work at it. Staff walk the head of the queue to the machine, so join the line first and buy when you are brought forward. The touch panel's main split is tsukemen versus chūka soba. ⚠ Before 10:00 the shop serves a morning-only menu and the regular bowls are not available; at dinner that does not apply.
rokurinsha.order: Tokusei tsukemen — very thick noodles served cold beside a dense, long-reduced pork-and-fish dipping broth, with extra pork and a soft egg on top.
rokurinsha.order_jp: 特製つけめんを ひとつ お願いします
rokurinsha.order_romaji: Tokusei tsukemen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
rokurinsha.order_why: This is the shop that made thick, heavily reduced tsukemen the Tokyo standard, and the tokusei is its own number-one seller — the plain tsukemen with shredded pork and a marinated egg already added, which is what most people end up wanting anyway. It is the longest queue on Tokyo Ramen Street and this is the bowl the queue is for.
rokurinsha.order_backup: Plain tsukemen (つけめん) is the same broth and noodles without the toppings. Chūka soba (中華そば) is the ordinary hot bowl and much the lighter order of the two.

kawashige-kamakura.order_how: Table service, forty seats — eight at the counter and thirty-two at tables — and walk-in. ⚑ The thing that makes it work at five in the afternoon: it runs straight through from eleven to eight with no break, so there is no opening rush to arrive into, and the kitchen's last order is seven. 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards. ⚑ Shirasu comes two ways and they are different dishes: nama (生, raw) and kama-age (釜揚げ, boiled). The raw one depends on that morning's catch and on the weather, so it is not always on; the boiled one always is.
kawashige-kamakura.order: Shirasu-don — Sagami Bay whitebait heaped over rice, the dish Kamakura is known for.
kawashige-kamakura.order_jp: しらす丼を ひとつ お願いします
kawashige-kamakura.order_why: The agriculture ministry lists nama-shirasu-don among Kanagawa's own regional dishes, and this shop takes its whitebait from Sagami Bay, which is the water in question. Late October falls inside the fishing season — 11 March to 31 December — and autumn is one of its two peaks, the autumn fish being the fatter of the two.
kawashige-kamakura.order_backup: The tempura bowls are what the house is actually built on: the large-prawn tendon (大海老天丼) and the house tendon (川茂天丼), both finished with the kaeshi handed down from the 1887 parent shop. There is also an eel bowl (うな丼) and a mixed seafood bowl (海鮮丼).

tenshinan.order_how: Table service in a converted house beside Kenchō-ji, with a garden room. Quieter and slower than anywhere else on this list — this is a sit-down lunch, not a queue-and-go.
tenshinan.order: Denshō kenchin-jiru — the root-vegetable and tofu soup said to have been created at Kenchō-ji next door, cooked to the temple's handed-down method.
tenshinan.order_jp: 伝承けんちん汁を ひとつ お願いします
tenshinan.order_romaji: Denshō kenchin-jiru o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tenshinan.order_why: Kenchin-jiru is eaten all over Japan, and the story of it starts at the temple you will have just walked through — the name is generally read as a corruption of Kenchō-ji. Ordering it here is the one place on the trip where the dish and the building that produced it are fifty metres apart.
tenshinan.order_backup: The soup is normally taken as part of a set with rice and sides rather than alone; if you want a plainer meal, the shop also serves a simple curry and a tofu course.

honke-daiichi-asahi.order_how: Order at the table — staff take it, no ticket machine. Cards and QR are accepted. Thirty-one seats, no reservations, and a queue outside at almost any hour, because it opens at six in the morning and runs past midnight. ⚠ Closed Thursdays.
honke-daiichi-asahi.order: Rāmen — thin straight noodles in a clear pork-and-soy broth, buried under sliced chāshū and a heap of green onion.
honke-daiichi-asahi.order_jp: ラーメンを ひとつ お願いします
honke-daiichi-asahi.order_why: This is the Kyoto bowl in its original form — the shop has been at the Takabashi corner since 1953 and the style it fixed is the one the rest of the city copied. The broth looks heavy and drinks light; the pork is the point.
honke-daiichi-asahi.order_backup: Tokusei rāmen (特製ラーメン) is the same bowl at roughly double: about five slices of chāshū instead of the usual few. ⚠ It is a great deal of pork for a late dinner — order it only if you skipped lunch.

kaidashimen-kitada.order_how: Order at the counter; cards and QR are accepted. Only eleven seats, no reservations. ⚑ It runs straight through from seven in the morning to ten at night with no midday break, which is what makes it the fallback whenever a day lands back in Kyoto at an hour when nothing else is serving.
kaidashimen-kitada.order: Kai-dashi men — ramen in a clear broth drawn entirely from shellfish: clams, scallops and their cousins, no pork at all.
kaidashimen-kitada.order_jp: 貝だし麺を ひとつ お願いします
kaidashimen-kitada.order_romaji: Kai-dashi men o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kaidashimen-kitada.order_why: The whole shop exists for this one idea, and it is the reason it is a Hyakumeiten pick — a shellfish broth is light in a way a pork broth never is, which is how the shop can trade from seven in the morning to ten at night without a break. ⚑ That fifteen-hour day is why it holds four slots on this trip — on each of them you arrive in the early evening with hours of service still ahead of you, which is the property the other candidates did not have.
kaidashimen-kitada.order_backup: Hamaguri rā-men (蛤らぁ麺), the clam-forward version, is the one regulars order second. A small bowl of shellfish simmered in soy over rice (貝のしぐれ煮ご飯) is the side to add if the ramen alone is not dinner.

yamamoto-mambo.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money, no QR. Cooked on the griddle in front of you and eaten off it, with about half the seats at the teppan. ⚠ The shop keeps no channel of its own, so its reservation policy is not recorded anywhere — treat it as walk-in.
yamamoto-mambo.order: Manbo-yaki — the house dish: a thin betayaki base with noodles, egg and everything else built on top, nothing like the Osaka or Hiroshima versions.
yamamoto-mambo.order_jp: まんぼ焼きを ひとつ お願いします
yamamoto-mambo.order_why: The shop has been open since 1948 and this dish is named after it — it is where manbo-yaki comes from, and Kyoto's own answer to okonomiyaki, which most people outside the city do not know exists. Ordering the plain betayaki here is ordering the thing without the reason for it.
yamamoto-mambo.order_backup: Beta-yaki (ベタ焼き) is the same base without the noodles piled in — lighter, and the better order if the day already had a big lunch.

arata.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money, no QR. Teppan cooking, fifty seats, reservations accepted. ⚠ Evenings only, from five, and closed Sundays.
arata.order: Arata okonomi — the house build in the manbo-yaki style: a thin base, coarse-cut cabbage and beansprouts, noodles, and agi, the sinewy meat from around the jaw.
arata.order_jp: あらたお好みを ひとつ お願いします
arata.order_romaji: Arata okonomi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
arata.order_why: Agi is what separates this from every other okonomiyaki on the trip — a cut most places will not bother with, slow enough to render that it turns the whole thing savoury. The shop has taken a Hyakumeiten place repeatedly on the strength of it.
arata.order_backup: Plain beta-yaki (ベタ焼き) without the agi is the milder order. The teppan meat dishes are well regarded in their own right if you would rather not eat another pancake.

moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_how: Proper table service on the 11th floor of the Isetan above Kyoto Station, with the city and its eastern hills through the window. 🔴 CASH OR CARD ONLY — the restaurant's own page states that electronic money and QR payment are not accepted, so an IC-only wallet fails here. ⚑ Walk in after 19:00: the floor's own rush is 18:00 to 19:00, last entry and last order are both 21:00, and a later sitting is the one with no line. ⚠ Lunch pricing stops at 16:00.
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order: Sukiyaki — kuroge wagyū cooked at the table in an iron pan with sugar and soy, then dipped in raw beaten egg.
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_jp: すき焼きを ひとつ お願いします
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_why: Morita-ya has been a Kyoto butcher since 1869 and raises its own cattle on a farm in Tanba, so the beef and the restaurant are the same business — which is the whole reason to eat sukiyaki here rather than anywhere cheaper. The set arrives as a sequence: an appetiser, the beef, vegetables and egg, then rice, red-miso soup, pickles and a dessert.
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_backup: Shabu-shabu is the same beef swirled through hot stock instead of simmered in soy — lighter and less sweet, and the order if the sugar-and-soy version sounds like too much after the day you have had. ⚑ Both of the evenings this shop is on are Kyoto in late autumn, so the sukiyaki is the seasonally obvious one. There is also an oil-yaki, essentially a steak.

wakakusa-curry.order_how: Order at the table; cards, Suica and QR are all accepted. Twenty-six seats, no reservations. ⚑ Two curries can be served side by side on one plate — ask for aigake (あいがけ) — which is the way to try the house curry without giving up a second one.
wakakusa-curry.order: Wakakusa curry — the house bowl: spinach, tomato, vegetables and minced meat cooked down into a thick, low-liquid, heavily spiced roux.
wakakusa-curry.order_jp: 若草カレーを ひとつ お願いします
wakakusa-curry.order_romaji: Wakakusa karē o hitotsu onegai shimasu
wakakusa-curry.order_why: The shop is named after this curry and it is the one that earned the Hyakumeiten place — dense and spice-forward rather than sweet, and much less oily than most Japanese curry. It sits about five minutes' walk from the Kintetsu station in a covered shopping street.
wakakusa-curry.order_backup: The chicken curry is creamy with coconut milk and the gentlest thing on the menu. Lamb brown curry (ラムブラウンカレー) is the opposite: thin, dark and genuinely hot. ⚑ If you cannot choose, aigake gives you two on one plate.

kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_how: Table and tatami seating, forty-three seats, cards and QR accepted, no reservations. 🔴 Each pot is cooked from raw after you order, so it takes roughly 20–25 minutes to arrive — this is not a quick lunch, and that is the trade for the crisp scorched crust at the bottom. ⚠ The times the shop publishes are LAST ORDERS rather than closing times, and the queue at midday can be an hour at weekends.
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order: Nara nanashu kamameshi — rice cooked to order in its own iron pot with seven toppings, among them prawn, crab and conger eel.
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_jp: 奈良七種釜めしを ひとつ お願いします
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_romaji: Nara nanashu kamameshi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_why: This has been the shop's number one since it opened more than sixty years ago, and it stands directly opposite the Nara National Museum, so it is the natural lunch on a museum day. Scrape the bottom of the pot — the scorched layer, okoge, is the part people come back for.
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_backup: The single-topping pots — conger eel, or mushroom in autumn — are lighter and cheaper, and cook in the same time.

icchan-honten.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no IC, no QR. A small room of counter, griddle-side and table seats, and dine-in reservations are not available at all, so it is walk-in by construction. ⚑ You are asked one question when you order — soba or udon in the pancake. Say soba; that is the Hiroshima default.
icchan-honten.order: Niku-tama soba — the standard Hiroshima build: a thin crêpe, a mountain of cabbage, pork belly, fried noodles and an egg, pressed together on the griddle.
icchan-honten.order_jp: 肉玉そばを ひとつ お願いします
icchan-honten.order_romaji: Niku-tama soba o hitotsu onegai shimasu
icchan-honten.order_why: Hiroshima okonomiyaki is layered, not mixed — that is the whole difference from Osaka — and niku-tama soba is the base every shop is judged on. This one has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand for six straight years and a Hyakumeiten place three times, run by the third generation of the same family.
icchan-honten.order_backup: The toppings go on the left side of the order: squid, squid tempura (イカ天), prawn, mochi or cheese. Squid tempura is the local one. Ask for udon instead of soba if you want it softer.

okonomiyaki-masaru.order_how: Cards are NOT accepted; QR payment is. Twenty seats, all of them at the counter around the iron plate — there are no tables, so you eat where it is cooked. ⚠ It does take reservations, unusually for an okonomiyaki shop, but the only channel on record for them is a telephone one — so plan on walking in, and go at the open rather than late. It runs lunch and then again from the evening.
okonomiyaki-masaru.order: Niku-tama soba — the layered Hiroshima pancake with pork and noodles, finished on the plate in front of you.
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_jp: 肉玉そばを ひとつ お願いします
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_romaji: Niku-tama soba o hitotsu onegai shimasu
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_why: This is the base bowl of the local style and the fair comparison against the other okonomiyaki on the trip. ⚑ The shop is also a teppanyaki counter and prices higher than a plain okonomiyaki-ya, so the griddle dishes are a real part of what you are paying for rather than a sideline.
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_backup: Order a teppanyaki dish alongside rather than instead — the griddle is the reason this place costs more than its neighbours. Squid tempura (イカ天) is the topping to add to the pancake.

kunimatsu-ekie.order_how: ⚠ Credit cards are NOT accepted, but Suica and nanaco are. Counter seats only, inside the ekie complex at Hiroshima Station, so it is reachable without leaving the building. No reservations.
kunimatsu-ekie.order: Half-and-half — one bowl split between the two shops' versions of shiru-nashi tantanmen, Hiroshima's soupless dandan noodles, with a soft egg and rice.
kunimatsu-ekie.order_jp: ハーフ＆ハーフを ひとつ お願いします
kunimatsu-ekie.order_romaji: Hāfu ando hāfu o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kunimatsu-ekie.order_why: This counter is a collaboration between two of the city's best-known shiru-nashi tantanmen shops, and the half-and-half exists so you can eat both side by side — Kunimatsu's sesame version against Musashibo's soy one. Ordering a single bowl here gives up the only reason this branch exists.
kunimatsu-ekie.order_backup: Either shop's bowl on its own if you would rather not compare. ⚑ Sichuan pepper, chilli oil, extra sauce and vinegar are on the table — the dish is meant to be adjusted, and stirring it thoroughly before the first mouthful is the local instruction. Rice refills are free.

yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_how: Cards and QR accepted, e-money not. Eighty-six seats across tables and tatami, ten minutes up the Omotesandō shopping street from the pier. Reservations are not being taken at present. 🔴 Last order is 16:30 — half an hour before the close, so the door time is not the ordering time.
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order: Both of them — yaki-gaki, oysters grilled in the shell over charcoal and opened at the table, and anago-meshi, conger eel over rice. ⚑ This shop does both of the island's dishes under one roof, which is exactly why the day needs no second stop after 535 metres of stone stairs.
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_jp: 焼がきを ひとつ お願いします
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_why: The shop opened in 1948 and is credited with being the first to sell grilled oysters to the public, which is why the dish is now the thing Miyajima is eaten for. It uses three-year oysters from Jigozen rather than the usual two-year ones, and they hold their flavour through the fire instead of shrinking away.
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_backup: The Itsukushima set puts raw oysters, oyster rice and fried oysters on one tray, and is the order if you want the oyster side of the menu rather than one of each. ⚑ There are also udon, soba and tonkatsu sets, if neither island dish appeals by the time you sit down.

kakiya-miyajima.order_how: Cards and QR accepted. A hundred and ten seats over two floors, no reservations, and it runs straight through from 10:00 to 18:00 rather than shutting mid-afternoon, which is why it is the backup. ⚠ It takes no fixed closing day but irregular closures do occur, and it may shut early once the day's oysters are gone. Look for the large white lantern on the Omotesandō.
kakiya-miyajima.order: Kakiya set — the house tray: oyster rice, fried oysters, oysters in oil, and an oyster miso soup.
kakiya-miyajima.order_jp: 牡蠣屋定食を ひとつ お願いします
kakiya-miyajima.order_romaji: Kakiya teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kakiya-miyajima.order_why: The set is how this shop shows what it does, which is oysters cooked five ways rather than one — a different proposition from the charcoal grill up the street, and the better order if you want to understand the ingredient rather than just eat it hot.
kakiya-miyajima.order_backup: Grilled oysters are sold single from the front of the shop if you only want one or two standing up. The oysters in oil (牡蠣のオイル漬け) are also sold to take away.

tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_how: Cards and QR accepted, e-money not. Forty seats with a tatami room, six minutes from Ryōgoku station down a quiet side street behind a red noren. ⚠ It takes dinner reservations — never lunch — and stops once the evening is full, so as a walk-in go early in the service rather than late.
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order: Toku-rōsu katsu — the premium loin cutlet, Hirata Bokujō pork, fried in fresh panko.
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_jp: 特ロースかつ定食を ひとつ お願いします
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_romaji: Toku-rōsu katsu teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_why: This is the shop's own headline cut and the reason it has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand every year since 2018 and a Hyakumeiten place repeatedly. ⚑ It is served with mustard, wasabi and salt rather than drowned in sauce — try a corner with salt alone before reaching for the bottle.
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_backup: The fillet cutlet (ヒレかつ) is the leaner order. ⚑ Ryōgoku is sumo country and the obvious thing to eat here is chanko — this is the deliberate alternative to it, on the day that already has chanko at lunch.

kyoto-yamaroku.order_how: Order at the table; cards and QR accepted, e-money not. Twenty-one seats in the basement of the Isetan attached to Kyoto Station, so it is reachable without going outside. No reservations, and it queues at midday. ⚠ It runs two services with the middle of the afternoon shut: lunch 11:00 to 15:00, then dinner 16:00 to 20:00.
kyoto-yamaroku.order: Saikyō-yaki set — fish cured in sweet white Kyoto miso and grilled, with four small vegetable dishes, rice and miso soup.
kyoto-yamaroku.order_jp: 西京焼き定食を ひとつ お願いします
kyoto-yamaroku.order_romaji: Saikyō-yaki teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kyoto-yamaroku.order_why: The parent company has been curing fish in saikyō miso for over ninety years and this is its first restaurant — you are eating the product at the source rather than a restaurant's version of it. The miso draws water out of the fish and sweetens it, so it grills to something denser than plain fish. Pick the sablefish (gindara) if it is offered: it is the one that goes soft rather than firm.
kyoto-yamaroku.order_backup: The set comes in several fish; whichever is on that day is the order. ⚑ The small side dishes are obanzai, the Kyoto home-cooking style, and are half the reason the set is worth having over a single grilled fish.

ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money, no QR. Ten seats, counter only, no reservations. It runs a lunch service and then a separate evening one, so it is shut through the middle of the afternoon.
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order: Ginjō miso tsukemen — thick noodles dipped into a miso broth built with sake lees, which is what the ginjō in the name refers to.
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_jp: 吟醸味噌つけ麺を ひとつ お願いします
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_romaji: Ginjō miso tsukemen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_why: Miso tsukemen is unusual anywhere and this shop is the reason to try it — a Hyakumeiten pick, and the sake-lees note makes it sweeter and rounder than the soy-based dipping broths elsewhere on this trip. Ordering the plain ramen here is ordering the thing it is not known for.
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_backup: Ginjō shōyu rāmen (吟醸醤油らーめん) is the orthodox soy bowl and the lighter meal of the two.

ami-ryogoku.order_how: Cards, Suica and QR all accepted — the easiest payment on this list. A hundred and twenty seats across tables, tatami and sunken hearths, reservations taken, and it runs continuously from 11:00 to midnight. ⚑ The pot is cooked at your table on a portable burner, so allow time. Lunch chanko sets are a fraction of the evening price.
ami-ryogoku.order: Chanko-nabe — the stew sumo stables cook for their wrestlers, here to a recipe handed down from the Isegahama stable, simmered at the table with chicken, seafood and vegetables.
ami-ryogoku.order_jp: ちゃんこ鍋を ひとつ お願いします
ami-ryogoku.order_why: Chanko is stable food rather than restaurant food, and eating it a few streets from the Kokugikan is the point of doing it in Ryōgoku at all. The chicken-based version is the traditional one — a stable eats chicken before a tournament because a chicken stands on two legs, and a wrestler on four has lost.
ami-ryogoku.order_backup: The seafood chanko is the lighter pot. ⚑ At the end, ask for rice or noodles to be cooked in what is left of the broth — that is how the stable finishes it, and it is where most of the flavour has ended up.

chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_how: Cards, Suica and QR accepted. Eighty-eight seats inside the Edo NOREN hall directly outside Ryōgoku station's west exit — the building with a full-size sumo ring in its atrium. Reservations taken. Cooked at the table.
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order: Kirishima chanko — the Mutsu stable's own recipe, a clear chicken-based pot finished at your table.
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_jp: ちゃんこ鍋を ひとつ お願いします
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_why: The restaurant belongs to a former ōzeki who now runs the Mutsu stable, and the pot is that stable's recipe rather than a general-purpose one. The building is worth the walk on its own: Edo NOREN keeps a regulation dohyō on the ground floor, which is the closest you will get to one without a tournament ticket.
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_backup: The hand-breaded fried chicken wings are the dish people order alongside and then remember. ⚑ Ask for the rice or noodles at the end, cooked in the remaining broth.

hiraso-horyuji.order_how: Table service, at the gate of Hōryū-ji — half shop, half restaurant, with a café counter as well. You can eat in and buy boxes to take away from the same building.
hiraso-horyuji.order: Nara lunch (奈良ランチ), the ¥2,000 set — five pieces of kakinoha-zushi, a bowl of thin nyūmen noodles in broth, a hot-spring egg, a small vegetable dish and a dessert. ⚑ Ask for it by name: it is the top set, and the price is what distinguishes it from the plainer trays.
hiraso-horyuji.order_jp: 奈良ランチを ひとつ お願いします
hiraso-horyuji.order_romaji: Nara ranchi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
hiraso-horyuji.order_why: Kakinoha-zushi is cured fish pressed onto vinegared rice and wrapped in a persimmon leaf — a mountain food invented to keep sea fish edible inland, and Hiraso is the sōhonke, the founding house of it. The set is the way to eat it as a meal rather than as a souvenir box.
hiraso-horyuji.order_backup: The plain kakinoha-zushi set — three mackerel, three salmon, with a clear soup — is the unadorned version. ⚑ The leaf is a wrapper, not food: unwrap it and leave it.

matsumotoya-horyuji.order_how: Table service, cards and QR accepted, a hundred and fifty seats — the large, easy option at the Hōryū-ji gate, and no reservations are needed. ⚠ It publishes no weekly closing day but states that it closes irregularly, so an open day cannot be asserted in advance.
matsumotoya-horyuji.order: Kaki udon — the shop's own invention: persimmon and persimmon leaf worked into the udon dough, served hot or cold.
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_jp: 柿うどんを ひとつ お願いします
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_romaji: Kaki udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_why: Hōryū-ji and persimmons are joined by the most famous haiku in Japan about eating one — Shiki's line about biting a persimmon as the temple bell rings — and this shop has built its whole menu on that association. The noodles are its own recipe and are not sold anywhere else.
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_backup: Tatsuta-age, marinated fried chicken, is the Ikaruga local dish and the thing to add if udon alone is not lunch. ⚑ The persimmon soft-serve afterwards is the same joke told a second way.

katsui-yamanobe.order_how: Proper table service in a yōshoku restaurant on the Yamanobe-no-michi — a sit-down meal in the middle of a walking day, so budget the time rather than expecting a counter.
katsui-yamanobe.order: Hamburg steak set — a ground-beef patty cooked and served on a hot iron plate, with rice, soup and sides.
katsui-yamanobe.order_jp: ハンバーグステーキ定食を ひとつ お願いします
katsui-yamanobe.order_romaji: Hanbāgu sutēki teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
katsui-yamanobe.order_why: Yōshoku is Japan's own century-old reworking of European cooking, and the hamburg steak is its central dish — this kitchen also does kuroge wagyū and beef stew at several times the price, which tells you the beef is taken seriously. The set is the affordable end of a serious menu.
katsui-yamanobe.order_backup: The prawn-fry set (エビフライ定食) is the other set at the same price. The charcoal-grilled wagyū set is the step up if the day deserves it.

picton-yanagimoto.order_how: A small canteen inside Yanagimoto station, run by the same people as the yōshoku restaurant up the road. Simple, quick and reliably open — which is the entire reason it is the backup here rather than a destination.
picton-yanagimoto.order: Whatever the day's set is — this is a station canteen, and the board by the counter is the menu.
picton-yanagimoto.order_jp: 本日のおすすめを ひとつ お願いします
picton-yanagimoto.order_romaji: Honjitsu no osusume o hitotsu onegai shimasu
picton-yanagimoto.order_why: It exists so the Yamanobe-no-michi walk has a hot meal that cannot fail — the value is that it is at the station and open, not that it is remarkable. ⚑ Because it shares a kitchen with Katsui up the road, the western-style dishes are better than a station canteen has any right to be.
picton-yanagimoto.order_backup: Ask what is quickest if the train time is tight — that phrase above simply asks for today's recommendation, which is the safest order in any canteen.

denbe-kibune.order_how: Seated strictly first-come, no reservations at all. 🔴 Assume cash: no channel on record states that this valley shop takes a card, so do not arrive without notes. ⛔ The riverbed platforms everyone photographs are a summer arrangement — in November you are eating indoors, and that is normal, not a disappointment.
denbe-kibune.order: Kamameshi — rice steamed to order in its own iron pot, served as a set with two small appetisers, pickles and soup.
denbe-kibune.order_jp: 釜めしを ひとつ お願いします
denbe-kibune.order_why: Kibune is a narrow cold valley of shrine and river, and its restaurants are mostly expensive kaiseki aimed at the summer riverbed trade. This is the one that stays plain and reasonable year-round, and the kamameshi is the dish it is known for — cooked from raw, so it takes time and comes out hot in a place that is genuinely cold in November.
denbe-kibune.order_backup: The soba is house-made and is the faster order: nishin soba with simmered herring, tororo with grated yam, or sansai with mountain vegetables. ⚑ Nishin soba is the Kyoto one.

kibune-club.order_how: A café rather than a restaurant — a wooden building in the valley serving hot drinks and light meals. Quieter than the soba houses and the better option if what you want is to sit down and get warm.
kibune-club.order: Kamameshi — rice steamed to order in its own pot. ⚑ Order the food, not the tea: you are here because the noodle house down the lane could not seat you, so this is lunch.
kibune-club.order_jp: 釜めしを ひとつ お願いします
kibune-club.order_why: This is a backup for a cold valley with very few options, and its value is comfort and a seat indoors. ⚑ Kibune in November is several degrees colder than central Kyoto and the walk from Kurama comes over a ridge — a hot drink here is worth more than it sounds.
kibune-club.order_backup: Matcha with a cake set, if the point is to stop rather than to eat.

suzuriishitei.order_how: 🔴 Assume cash — nothing on record says a Takao teahouse takes a card, and the day's gates are cash too. A mountain teahouse on the path between the Takao bridge and Jingo-ji's steps. Order at the counter and sit on the benches.
suzuriishitei.order: Yuba soba — buckwheat noodles in hot broth with sheets of tofu skin, which is a Kyoto ingredient rather than a garnish.
suzuriishitei.order_jp: 湯葉そばを ひとつ お願いします
suzuriishitei.order_romaji: Yuba soba o hitotsu onegai shimasu
suzuriishitei.order_why: It sits exactly where you will want to sit down — at the bottom of the Jingo-ji staircase, either bracing for it or recovering from it — and a hot bowl is the right thing at that moment in November. Yuba is skimmed off simmering soy milk and is one of the few genuinely Kyoto things on a plate.
suzuriishitei.order_backup: ⚑ The thing the shop is actually famous for is momiji mochi, a maple-leaf rice cake, taken with matcha — order that instead if you only want to stop for ten minutes rather than eat.

takao-chaya.order_how: A mountain teahouse by the Kiyotaki river below Takao, everything handmade on site. Order at the counter. ⚑ It runs a full kaiseki business as well, so be clear you want the simple set rather than a course.
takao-chaya.order: Yudōfu set — blocks of tofu simmered in a clay pot of hot broth at your table, with rice and sides.
takao-chaya.order_jp: 湯どうふ定食を ひとつ お願いします
takao-chaya.order_romaji: Yudōfu teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
takao-chaya.order_why: The shop names this itself as what it recommends once the weather turns cold, and early November on this river is cold. Yudōfu is a Kyoto temple dish — almost nothing but tofu, water and kombu — and it is far better than that description sounds when eaten outdoors in the cold.
takao-chaya.order_backup: Momiji udon or soba with yuzu (柚子入もみじうどん) is the lighter, quicker order, and the two-colour soba set with seasonal rice is the bigger one. ⚑ The udon, the soba and the rice cakes are all made in the building.

yakko-yoshino.order_how: Table and tatami seating, sixty-three seats, no reservations, directly in front of Kinpusen-ji. 🔴 JCB is the only card accepted, so carry cash for this one.
yakko-yoshino.order: Kakinoha-zushi — salt-cured mackerel or salmon pressed on vinegared rice and wrapped in a persimmon leaf.
yakko-yoshino.order_jp: 柿の葉寿司を ひとつ お願いします
yakko-yoshino.order_why: This is one of the oldest houses making it, and it cures its fish in salt rather than vinegar — the older method, and noticeably firmer and less sharp than the versions sold at stations. Eating it in Yoshino, where the technique comes from, is the difference between the dish and a souvenir of it.
yakko-yoshino.order_backup: Kuzu udon — noodles in a broth thickened with Yoshino arrowroot until it turns glossy — is the local speciality and the warmer order on a ridge in November. ⚑ Order both: the sushi travels, the udon does not.

harukaze-yoshino.order_how: A small eating house on the Yoshino ridge road. Simple, table service, and its value is that it is open on a stretch where most things are not.
harukaze-yoshino.order: Kuzu udon — udon in a broth thickened with Yoshino arrowroot starch, which turns it glossy and holds the heat.
harukaze-yoshino.order_jp: 葛うどんを ひとつ お願いします
harukaze-yoshino.order_romaji: Kuzu udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
harukaze-yoshino.order_why: Yoshino kuzu is the arrowroot the whole region is known for, and thickening a hot broth with it is the local way to eat it savoury rather than as a sweet. On a cold ridge walk it stays hot far longer than a plain broth would, which is the actual reason the dish exists here.
harukaze-yoshino.order_backup: Kakinoha-zushi, the persimmon-leaf sushi, is the other Yoshino thing and is sold here too.

tsukumo-udon.order_how: Order at the counter; cards, Suica and QR all accepted. Thirty-five seats on the second basement level of Kyoto Station, between the subway and the JR lines. ⚑ Open 07:00 to 22:00 every day — this is the one that is always open when a day runs long.
tsukumo-udon.order: Keiran udon — udon in an iriko broth with egg stirred through it until the soup turns cloudy and soft.
tsukumo-udon.order_jp: 鶏卵うどんを ひとつ お願いします
tsukumo-udon.order_romaji: Keiran udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tsukumo-udon.order_why: The broth is built on iriko, dried sardines from Kujūkushima, which gives it a deeper and slightly sweeter base than the kelp-only broth most Kyoto udon uses, and the noodles are made in house. The egg version is the shop's most ordered bowl and the most forgiving thing to eat late.
tsukumo-udon.order_backup: The plain hot or cold iriko bowls show the broth with nothing in the way. The curry udon is the heavier order if the day was long and cold.

ekibenya-matsuri.order_how: ⛔ Not a restaurant — a shop. Take a box off the shelf, queue at the till, pay with Suica or a card. Nothing is spoken and nothing is cooked to order. ⚑ Ask for chopsticks if none are handed over: 「お箸をください」 (o-hashi o kudasai).
ekibenya-matsuri.order: Whichever box you want — around a hundred and fifty kinds, from all over the country, restocked through the day.
ekibenya-matsuri.order_jp: これを ひとつ お願いします
ekibenya-matsuri.order_why: This is the largest ekiben counter in Japan and the point is the choice, not a particular box — regional bento from lines that end nowhere near Tokyo are sold here and nowhere else in the city. ⚑ Buy something from where you are going or where you have been; that is what the format is for.
ekibenya-matsuri.order_backup: ⚑ The phrase above is for pointing at something behind glass. If a box can be heated the staff will ask you — the question is atatamemasu ka (温めますか), shall I warm it, and yes is hai (はい).

ekibenya-odori.order_how: ⛔ Not a restaurant — a shop, ten metres further along the same walk. Take a box, pay at the till, cards and Suica accepted. ⚑ Smaller and more curated than its neighbour, so the queue is usually shorter.
ekibenya-odori.order: Whichever box you want — a selected range rather than the full national spread.
ekibenya-odori.order_jp: これを ひとつ お願いします
ekibenya-odori.order_why: It exists as the edited version of the counter beside it: fewer boxes, chosen rather than comprehensive. ⚑ That makes it the better stop when the first one is three deep and the train is soon — which is exactly the situation it is listed for.
ekibenya-odori.order_backup: ⚑ Whatever is bought, buy it BEFORE passing through the Shinkansen transfer gate — both counters sit outside it.

yumehyakusen-ekie.order_how: ⛔ Not a restaurant — a souvenir and bento hall on the second floor of ekie at Hiroshima Station. Take a box, pay at the till. ⚑ It is OUTSIDE the ticket gates, so buy before you go through; once you are in, it is behind you.
yumehyakusen-ekie.order: Anago-meshi — conger eel, grilled and laid over rice cooked in its stock. The box from Ueno at Miyajimaguchi is the one to look for.
yumehyakusen-ekie.order_jp: あなごめしを ひとつ お願いします
yumehyakusen-ekie.order_why: Anago-meshi is the dish of this stretch of coast, and Ueno has been selling this box since 1901, when it began as the station bento for the Miyajima line — you will have spent the previous day on the island it is named after. ⚠ Deliveries come in from Miyajimaguchi and can sell out, so this is a preference, not a plan.
yumehyakusen-ekie.order_backup: If the anago box has gone, any of the other counters in the hall will do — the day has about ninety minutes of slack here, so nothing about this stop is rushed.

ethiopia-akihabara.order_how: Table service inside Atre at Akihabara station, so it is reachable without going outside. 🔴 You are asked one question and it matters: how hot, on a scale that runs from 0 to 70. ⚑ Say 「3ばい」 (san-bai, three times) for a normal hot; anything past 10 is a decision, not a preference. Steamed potatoes come free with the curry and can be refilled.
ethiopia-akihabara.order: Chicken curry — a thin, twelve-spice curry with vegetables and pulses cooked down into it.
ethiopia-akihabara.order_jp: チキンカレーを 3ばいで お願いします
ethiopia-akihabara.order_romaji: Chikin karē o san-bai de onegai shimasu
ethiopia-akihabara.order_why: The house has been making this since 1988 in Jinbōchō and it is one of the reference points for Japanese-style spice curry. The roux is built on twelve spices with vegetables and beans cooked to nothing, so it tastes deep rather than merely hot even at the low numbers.
ethiopia-akihabara.order_backup: Beef, pork-and-vegetable, prawn and bean curries are all on the same menu at the same heat scale. ⚠ The scale is real: the shop will go past 70 on request and there is no reason to find out.

meals.time_hint: Arrival night — no clock on it. The first rung walks straight in; the better bowl below it has a line

restaurants.note: Inside Atre Akihabara 1 at the station, 150 m from the hotel and reachable without going outside. Open to 22:30, last order 22:00, so there is no hour at which you are too late. Table service, no reservations, and no queue on record — which on this night is the whole point. Cards and IC. ⚠ It publishes no closing day of its own and follows Atre's calendar, which is on the recheck list for about 8 October.

The better bowl and the reason this night was built around it — but the way in is a line, about ten people and 15–20 minutes on a normal evening. It is a minute from the station on the same walk, so you can look at the door and decide. ⚠ Dinner is 18:00 to 21:30, and one channel prints 21:00 instead. If the line is there, Atre is 150 m on and Kamayoshi ten minutes the other way.

meals.time_hint: On the walk home, in Akihabara

restaurants.note: Last order 20:00, an hour before the close. Six minutes from the hotel. ⚠ The shop keeps no channel of its own — no site, no social account — so its hours cannot be confirmed before you fly; keep the backup live.

🔴 Only worth the walk if you decide early. Both kitchens last-order at 20:00 and this one is eight minutes further along the same walk, so leave Marugo's queue by about 19:00 or not at all. After that, go to a later-closing venue instead: Ethiopia Curry Kitchen (エチオピア) in Atre Akihabara, last order 22:00, 150 m from the hotel and on the walk home.

days.subtitle: the Tokyo splurge, and the one night with a fork

meals.time_hint: On the way home, along Ueno-Hirokōji

restaurants.note: Last order 19:45. 🔴 Tonight's fork: on Saturdays both Ueno museums stay open to 20:00, and 19:45 is fifteen minutes the wrong side of that — the museums and this table cannot both happen. If you take the museums, the backup below serves to 21:30.

On the same Ueno-Hirokōji block as Ponta, on the way home, and serving to 21:30 — which is what makes it the answer if the museums run to 20:00. ⚑ It is also tomorrow's first choice: eating it tonight moves Sunday to Mendokoro Honda.

meals.time_hint: Anchored to the hotel end — the day has no fixed evening position

restaurants.note: Ten minutes on foot from the hotel. ⚑ If you ate here last night — Saturday's museum fork can put it there — tonight moves to Mendokoro Honda, the backup below.
Eighteen seats and a slow turnover, so a line of about ten and a 15–20 minute wait is the normal evening — but it is 150 m from the hotel, so waiting tonight costs nothing else.

days.subtitle: something easy, on the way home

meals.time_hint: At the summit, roughly 12:30–13:30

restaurants.note: ⛔ There is no lunch on this mountain that can be relied on in advance — all three houses close irregularly, and each says so itself. Yamabiko-chaya (やまびこ茶屋), one level below the summit plaza and trading there since 1945, opens 10:00–15:00 and prints its closing days as irregular. Ōmiharashi-tei (大見晴亭), the highest teahouse, in the middle of the summit plaza, opens 10:00–16:00, closes Thursdays and also shuts for weather. Takahashiya (髙橋家) beside the cable car's Kiyotaki station, founded in the late Edo period and the source of the mountain's signature tororo soba, is reachable on the descent around 15:00–16:00 — but its hours are inconsistent and it is irregular too. ⇒ Buy onigiri or sandwiches at the Akihabara konbini before boarding; eat them on the summit deck if the houses are shut, and treat a hot bowl of tororo soba as the upside rather than the plan. ⚑ Takahashiya is an alternative to the Shinjuku dinner below, not an addition to it — and the stop costs more than the bowl: sitting down here is what makes you miss the 16:30 door in Shinjuku, so treat it as choosing this meal over that one.

meals.time_hint: 🔴 The clock decides where you eat, not whether — Shinjuku if you are at the door before 16:30, otherwise by the hotel

restaurants.note: 🔴 THE HOUR IS THE WHOLE DECISION, and you can settle it on the platform at Takaosanguchi. Fourteen counter seats: reports put no wait at all before 16:30, eight people ahead at 16:50 (seated about 17:10), a line out on the street just after 17:00, and thirty-five minutes at 19:25. ⇒ If the descent goes to plan you reach Shinjuku about 16:00 and walk straight in. ⛔ If you are not going to be at the door by about half four — a slow descent, a bowl of soba at Takahashiya, a long stop at the summit — do not come here; take the Ethiopia branch below instead. ⚠ Check the walk before you set off: the nearest stations are Shinjuku-sanchōme and Shinjuku-gyoenmae, not JR Shinjuku. Shinjuku is the Keiō interchange you change at anyway, so it is on the route — but allow more than four minutes for it after three hours on the mountain.

🔴 THE BRANCH THAT WORKS AT ANY HOUR, and the one to take if you are off the mountain later than planned. Table service, no queue on record, open until 22:30 with last order at 22:00, cards and IC accepted — and it is in Atre at Akihabara station, 150 m from the hotel and on the walk home, so it costs no detour at all. ⇒ You do not have to decide before you board: if you reach Shinjuku after about half four, stay on the train.

restaurants.cuisine: Indian street food and spice curry
restaurants.note: ⛔ NOT the answer if the first choice has a line, because at that hour it is shut: it closes 15:00–17:00, which is exactly when this day reaches Shinjuku. And 17:00 is its reopening, not a quiet moment — a listing calls it a shop people queue at before it opens. ⚠ Nobody has published a wait in minutes for it at any hour, so this is a named rung, not a measured one. It earns its place on the other things: twenty-nine seats with table service rather than a counter, and cards, IC and QR all accepted — the day's one cashless way out, on a day whose lunch and first choice are both cash. Five minutes from Seibu-Shinjuku, about ten from the Keiō concourse. ⇒ Use it only if you are eating in Shinjuku at 17:30 or later and are content to take a queue you cannot size in advance.

days.subtitle: something easy, on the way home

restaurants.cuisine: Kenchin-jiru, the soup invented at Kenchō-ji

meals.time_hint: Eat in Kamakura about 17:00, before the train home — the backup below is back in Tokyo, at the station you change at

restaurants.note: 🔴 Eat before the train, not after it — that single change is what solves this evening. Tokyo Station at a quarter to seven is the dinner peak, and every good specialist near it is a small counter: the three that were measured came back at thirty minutes, fifteen to twenty, and ten just to be seated. Kamakura at five o'clock is the opposite. The day walks out of Tsurugaoka Hachimangū and straight down Komachi-dōri, the tour crowds have gone home, and this shop is three minutes from the east exit with the station right behind it. ✅ Why this one and not the rest of the street: almost all of Komachi-dōri shuts around half past five, and this runs eleven to eight straight through with last order at seven, so it is still serving long after the neighbours have closed. Forty seats and table service. ⚠ Aim to sit down a little after five rather than before it: two of its channels print that continuous band, but a third prints a midday break and a five o'clock reopen — arriving after five works whichever is right, and arriving at half past four may not. Founded as the sister of an 1887 house; the whitebait is landed in Sagami Bay and late October is the fatter of the two shirasu seasons. Shirasu bowl ¥1,430, large-prawn tendon ¥2,100, house tendon ¥3,500. 🔴 Cash only. ⚠ Closed Wednesdays — this is a Tuesday. ⚑ Nothing on the day depends on the raw shirasu: if the catch or the weather went against it that morning, the boiled version and the tempura bowls are the house's real backbone anyway. ⚑ One honest gap: unlike almost every other name in this file, no rating site scores this shop and it holds no Hyakumeiten or Michelin listing — it was chosen on the house record, the city tourism association's listing and the hours, not on a score.

🔴 Only if Kamakura fell through — or if you would rather have the bowl and pay for it in time. This is the shop that made thick, heavily reduced tsukemen the Tokyo standard, and it sits on Tokyo Ramen Street at the station you change at, so it costs no detour to look. What it costs in minutes is measured, at every hour it trades: about thirty at the dinner peak, thirty at lunch, forty-five on a holiday, and twenty even after nine at night, its quietest evening hour. The only no-wait window on record is half past three to four, which is not a dinner. ⚑ So this is yours to decide at the door rather than mine to plan — nothing in the day is built on it. Last order 22:30. ⛔ Nippon Ramen Rin, a level below on Gransta's Ginno-suzu, is the other name down there and it is not the shortcut it looks like: fifteen counter seats, numbered tickets handed out when busy, and nobody publishes what it does at the dinner peak. ✅ The no-queue way out, if you get back hungry and cannot face either: Ethiopia Curry in Atre Akihabara, 150 m from the hotel, last order 22:00 — it is night 1's primary, so you will already know it.

restaurants.note: At the Jingo-ji end of the lane, so you pass it coming away from the temple, before the primary. ⚠ Its closing days are irregular, and the rule that clears today — no closures at all from October to early December — comes from the Takao preservation association rather than from the shop, which publishes nothing itself. ⚑ Two more options stand behind this one, and they cannot fail the same way the teahouses can. And Togano-chaya (とがの茶屋) sits at Kōzan-ji, which is the day's exit rather than its lunch point: 9:00 to 17:00, no closures from 20 October to 30 November. Not a lunch option but a late-afternoon one before the bus, which matters because the wait at the Toganoo stop runs 10 to 20 minutes.

Taking it means arriving at Yakko earlier, not later.

Thirty seconds along the street from the primary, and the latest close on Miyajima — which is exactly what makes it survive a badly delayed descent. restaurants.note: Ten minutes on foot from the hotel, inside the home district, three minutes from Awajichō. It opens at 17:30 and last-orders at 20:00 — twenty minutes before the close, and the earliest last order on the trip — while you are back at the hotel about 16:55 with nothing after it. ⚠ The shop asks you to check its own social account for the days it trades, so an open day cannot be assumed; it also stops when the noodles run out.

About 150 metres from the hotel, on the first floor of Atre Akihabara 1 — on the walk home from the Shinkansen arrival, so no transfer and no separate leg. Last order 22:00; cards and IC, no reservations. ⚡ That puts two hours behind the primary's 20:00 last order, so if the Shinkansen slips or the November calendar closes the primary, the night still eats 150 metres from the bed. ⚠ Neither of its own channels states a closing day, so it follows Atre's calendar — on the recheck list for about 8 October, and it matters more tonight than on the earlier nights, because here it is the second name rather than the third.

meals.time_hint: In Ryōgoku, about 12:30 — between the station and the Edo-Tokyo Museum

restaurants.note: One minute from Ryōgoku's JR east exit, 103 metres, on the 2nd and 3rd floors; the lunch service runs 11:00 to 15:00. ⚠ It is bookable online as well as walk-in, so it can be full — and what answers that is the room itself: a hundred and twenty seats across tables, tatami and sunken hearths, at half past twelve on an ordinary Tuesday. ⇒ This slot stands on the seat count, not on the names below it. ⚑ Read the 3.47 against other chanko, not against Ryōgoku at large: eighteen chanko houses sit within about 500 metres of the station, the best of them reaches 3.53, and none appears in the district's top 20. ⚠ The stable-recipe claim appears in editorial copy rather than on the shop's own page. ⚑ A third name if both of the first two fail: Sumo Chaya Terao (相撲茶屋 寺尾), 3.47 on 275 reviews, 173 metres — run by a former wrestler who is the elder brother of the Terao it is named for, not by Terao himself. ⚠ Unlike the two above it, nothing about this one was checked — not its seats, not its closing day, not its hours. It is a name to walk to, not a verified fallback.

42 metres from Ryōgoku's west exit and on the same block as the Edo-Tokyo Museum — it sits literally between the station and the museum. Lunch last order is 14:00, an hour before the close, and it seats 88 at tables — so like the primary, this one answers a busy day with the size of the room rather than with a wait. ⚠ The only closing rule either channel publishes is a summer one, so treat November as unknown. 🔴 Do not confuse it with the other branch: Kirishima's honten, 97 metres away, is the highest-rated of them all with a lunch at 3.49 — and it is closed Mondays and Tuesdays, so it is dead on this date. Two branches of one name with different closing days.

meals.time_hint: Back at Ryōgoku about 17:15, or about 18:00 if the Kiyosumi garden coda is taken — a table around 17:45–18:15

restaurants.note: On Yokozuna Yokochō, off Ryōgoku's east exit. Last order 22:00 — which makes the Kiyosumi detour free: back at Ryōgoku about 18:00 with it, about 17:15 without, and neither competes with dinner. ✅ Its own site says open all year with only a new-year closure and publishes no irregular-closure clause at all, so this is the rare venue that needs no pre-trip check. ⚖ The upside option, offered rather than quietly dropped: Teuchi Ren (手打式 らぁ麺 蓮), 3.87 with a two-year award listing, is the highest score in the corridor — eight minutes on foot and six from Morishita, so it sits on the Kiyosumi axis rather than off it, 17:00 to 22:00, closed Mondays. 🔴 Take it only if there is no line: seven seats, cash only, and the shop states that waiting inside is not permitted. On the last night, with no following day to absorb a failed walk-in, that is an upside bet and not a fallback. ⚑ The kanji is 蓮, not 練 — the wrong character will not find it on the ground.

At Akihabara, two Sōbu stops from Ryōgoku and about four minutes — and 150 metres from the hotel, so it is also the answer if you simply ride straight home. ⚑ But check the clock before you ride: its evening service does not open until 18:00, so on the early version of this day — back at Ryōgoku about 17:15, at Akihabara by about 17:25 — you would be standing outside it. Either take the Kiyosumi garden coda and arrive after six, or eat at the primary in Ryōgoku, which is already serving.
